q-pn-case.label: Subject and object forms
q-pn-case.summary: I, he, she, we, they do the action; me, him, her, us, them receive it or follow a preposition.

q-pn-agree.label: Agreement with the noun it stands for
q-pn-agree.summary: Each, every, everyone, nobody and a singular noun take a singular pronoun.

q-pn-reflexive.label: Myself, himself, themselves
q-pn-reflexive.summary: A reflexive is used only when the doer and the receiver are the same, or for emphasis.

q-pn-relative.label: Relative pronouns
q-pn-relative.summary: Who for people, which for things, that for either, whose for possession, whom as an object.

q-pn-order.label: Order of pronouns in one sentence
q-pn-order.summary: When 'I', 'you' and 'he/she' share a sentence: good news or a plain statement goes 2nd-3rd-1st person (you, he and I); admitting a fault goes 1st-2nd-3rd (I, you and he).

q-pn-possform.label: No apostrophe in a possessive pronoun
q-pn-possform.summary: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: its, yours, hers, theirs, ours — never it's, your's, her's.

q-pn-each.label: Two people vs more than two
q-pn-each.summary: 'Each other' is for exactly two; 'one another' is for more than two.

rules.text: After a preposition, and as the object of a verb, use the object form: between you and me, for him and me. The subject form (I, he, she, we, they) is used only when the pronoun does the action.
rules.ok: Between you and me; he invited my brother and me.
rules.bad: Between you and I; he invited my brother and I.

rules.text: After 'than' and 'as ... as' in a comparison, the pronoun takes the form it would have if the verb were written out: she is taller than I (am), not than me, in formal use.
rules.ok: He works harder than I do.
rules.bad: He works harder than me do.

rules.text: Each, every, everyone, everybody, nobody, anyone, either and neither are singular, so the pronoun that refers back is his, her or his or her, and the verb is singular.
rules.ok: Everyone must bring his or her own pen.
rules.bad: Everyone must bring their own pen (in exam grammar).

rules.text: A reflexive (myself, himself, themselves) is correct only when it refers back to the subject of the same clause, or when it is added for emphasis. It is never used in place of a plain subject or object pronoun.
rules.ok: He hurt himself. I myself saw it.
rules.bad: Myself will attend. He invited my friend and myself.

rules.text: Use 'who' for people and 'which' for things; 'that' can do either but is not used after a comma. 'Whom' is the object form, used after a verb or a preposition.
rules.ok: The officer who signed it; the file which was lost; the man to whom I spoke.
rules.bad: The officer which signed it; the man to who I spoke.

rules.text: Make sure a pronoun has exactly one possible noun to refer to. If two nouns could be meant, name the noun again instead of using a pronoun.
rules.ok: When Ravi met Arun, Ravi was in a hurry.
rules.bad: When Ravi met Arun, he was in a hurry (who was?).

rules.text: When 'I', 'you' and 'he/she' appear together as subjects, the order depends on the sentence's sense. For ordinary statements or good news, use 2nd-3rd-1st person: you, he and I. For admitting a fault or something unwelcome, use 1st-2nd-3rd person: I, you and he.
rules.ok: You, he and I have won the quiz.
rules.bad: I, you and he have won the quiz (good news should put 'I' last).

rules.text: A possessive pronoun never takes an apostrophe: its, yours, hers, ours, theirs. 'It's' (with an apostrophe) always means 'it is' or 'it has', never 'belonging to it'.
'Each other' refers to exactly two people or things; 'one another' refers to more than two. Careful written English keeps this distinction, even though everyday speech often blurs it.
rules.ok: The two brothers help each other. All five members trust one another.
rules.bad: All five members trust each other (more than two, so 'one another' is preferred).

q-pn-case.cue: A blank or an underlined pronoun after a preposition, after 'and', or after 'than'.
q-pn-case.standard: Drop the other name and read the sentence with the pronoun alone: 'he invited me' tells you at once that 'me' is right.
q-pn-case.fast: A pronoun straight after a preposition is always the object form.
q-pn-case.eliminate: Cross out the subject forms whenever the pronoun is not doing the action.
traps: 'Between you and I' sounds polite but is wrong.
'Than me' and 'than I' differ; exam keys take the subject form in formal comparison.

q-pn-agree.cue: Everyone, each, nobody or a singular noun early in the sentence, with a pronoun later.
q-pn-agree.standard: Find the noun the pronoun stands for and match its number and person.
q-pn-agree.eliminate: Drop plural pronouns when the noun they point back to is singular.
traps: 'Their' after 'everyone' is normal in speech but marked wrong in these papers.
A plural noun inside an 'of' phrase pulls the pronoun to the plural.

q-pn-reflexive.cue: Myself, himself or themselves in a place where a plain pronoun would do.
q-pn-reflexive.standard: Check whether the reflexive refers back to the subject of its own clause. If not, replace it with I, me, he or him.
q-pn-reflexive.fast: No subject to refer back to means no reflexive.
q-pn-reflexive.eliminate: Remove options that use a reflexive as a subject.
traps: 'Myself' used politely as a subject or after 'and'.
'Themself' is not used in these papers; 'themselves' is.

q-pn-relative.cue: A blank joining two clauses, with who, whom, which, that or whose among the options.
q-pn-relative.standard: Decide whether the noun before the blank is a person or a thing, then whether the pronoun is the subject or the object of its clause.
q-pn-relative.fast: A verb straight after the blank means the subject form (who); a subject straight after means the object form (whom).
q-pn-relative.eliminate: Drop 'that' after a comma and 'which' after a person.
traps: 'Who' used where 'whom' is needed after a preposition.
A pronoun with two possible nouns to refer to.

q-pn-order.cue: 'I', 'you' and 'he'/'she' (or their names) listed together as the subject of one sentence.
q-pn-order.standard: Decide whether the sentence announces something good/neutral or admits a fault, then order the pronouns 2-3-1 or 1-2-3 accordingly.
q-pn-order.fast: Good news: you, he, I. Bad news/fault: I, you, he.
q-pn-order.eliminate: Drop any option that puts 'I' first in good news, or last when a fault is being admitted.
traps: Listing the pronouns in whatever order they come to mind, rather than by this fixed rule.
Politely putting 'I' last even when the sentence is admitting a mistake, where it should come first.

q-pn-possform.cue: its, your, her, our or their followed by an apostrophe-s, or 'it's' where possession is meant.
q-pn-possform.standard: Check whether the sentence means 'belonging to' (no apostrophe) or 'is/has' (apostrophe, only for it's).
q-pn-possform.fast: No possessive pronoun ever takes an apostrophe.
q-pn-possform.eliminate: Drop every option with an apostrophe unless the sentence means 'it is' or 'it has'.
traps: 'It's' meaning 'belonging to it', which is always wrong.
'Your's' and 'her's', which do not exist in standard English at all.

q-pn-each.cue: Two or more people/things doing something to or for each other.
q-pn-each.standard: Count how many are involved. Exactly two takes 'each other'; more than two takes 'one another'.
q-pn-each.fast: Two = each other. Three or more = one another.
q-pn-each.eliminate: Drop 'each other' once the sentence names more than two people or things.
traps: Using 'each other' by habit even when the sentence clearly names three or more participants.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
This matter is strictly between you and ___.
practice.why: After the preposition 'between' the object form is needed: between you and me.

a.note: 'Between you and I' is the best-known error of this kind; 'between' is a preposition and takes 'me'.

c.note: 'Myself' has no subject in this clause to refer back to, so a reflexive cannot be used here.

d.note: 'Mine' is possessive and would mean 'the thing belonging to me'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The principal congratulated my partner and ___ on the result.
practice.why: Drop 'my partner and' and the sentence reads 'congratulated me', so the object form is right.

a.note: 'And I' is chosen because it sounds more careful, but the pronoun here receives the action.

c.note: A reflexive after 'and' is a common politeness error; the subject of the clause is the principal, not me.

d.note: 'Mine' is possessive and does not fit as the object of 'congratulated'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
Each of the candidates must bring ___ own documents.
practice.why: 'Each' is singular, so the pronoun referring back to it is singular.

a.note: 'Their' after 'each' is normal in speech, but these papers treat 'each' as singular.

c.note: 'Them' is an object form and cannot stand before 'own documents'.

d.note: 'Theirs' is possessive and stands alone, so it cannot be followed by a noun.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
Every student in the two sections / has submitted their assignment / to the class teacher / before the deadline.
options: Every student in the two sections
practice.why: 'Every student' is singular, so the pronoun must be 'his or her assignment'.

a.note: 'Every student in the two sections' is a correctly built singular subject.

c.note: 'To the class teacher' is a prepositional phrase and holds no pronoun error.

d.note: 'Before the deadline' is a phrase of time.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
[[Myself and my brother]] will attend the function.
practice.why: The pronoun is the subject, so it takes 'I', and the courteous order puts the other person first.

b.note: 'Myself' cannot be a subject; there is no earlier subject for it to refer back to.

c.note: 'Me' is the object form and cannot be the subject of 'will attend'.

d.note: A reflexive after 'and' is still a reflexive with nothing to refer back to.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The manager asked the clerk / to send the papers / to the auditor and myself / by Friday evening.
practice.why: The subject of the clause is 'the clerk', not the speaker, so the reflexive has nothing to refer back to; it should be 'and me'.

a.note: 'The manager asked the clerk' is a correct main clause.

b.note: 'To send the papers' is a correct infinitive with its object.

d.note: 'By Friday evening' is a phrase of time.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The officer ___ signed the order has been transferred.
practice.why: The noun is a person and the pronoun is the subject of 'signed', so 'who' is right.

a.note: 'Which' is used for things, not for a person.

c.note: 'Whom' is the object form, but here the pronoun does the signing.

d.note: 'Whose' shows possession and would need a noun after it.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
This is the colleague to ___ I handed the file.
practice.why: After a preposition the object form is used: to whom I handed the file.

a.note: 'To who' keeps the subject form after a preposition, which formal grammar does not allow.

c.note: 'Which' is for things, and a colleague is a person.

d.note: 'Whose' shows possession and would need a noun after it.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
When Ravi met Arun, [[he was in a hurry]].
options: he himself was in a hurry
that he was in a hurry
practice.why: 'He' could mean either man, so the noun is repeated to make the reference certain.

b.note: Leaving 'he' in keeps the ambiguity: either Ravi or Arun could be meant.

c.note: Adding 'himself' emphasises the pronoun but still does not say which man is meant.

d.note: 'That he was in a hurry' turns the clause into a noun clause with nothing to attach to.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
My sister sings far better than ___.
practice.why: The comparison is with the full clause 'than I do', so the subject form is used in formal grammar.

a.note: 'Than me' is normal in conversation, but exam keys expect the form that would stand before the understood verb.

c.note: A reflexive has nothing to refer back to in this clause.

d.note: 'Mine' is possessive and would compare her singing with a thing of mine.

practice.caution: Everyday English allows 'than me'. These papers follow the older rule, which supplies the verb: than I (do).

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
Neither of the two sisters has brought [[their]] certificate.
practice.why: 'Neither' is singular and both people are women, so the pronoun is 'her'.

b.note: 'Their' is plural and does not agree with the singular 'neither'.

c.note: 'Theirs' stands alone and cannot be followed by 'certificate'.

d.note: This mixes two pronouns together and is not possible English.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The committee rejected the proposal, / that had been submitted / without the supporting papers, / at its first meeting.
practice.why: 'That' is not used after a comma; the clause adds information, so it needs 'which had been submitted'.

a.note: 'The committee rejected the proposal' is a correct main clause.

c.note: 'Without the supporting papers' is a correct prepositional phrase.

d.note: 'At its first meeting' is correct, with a singular pronoun for the committee.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
___ have won the inter-school quiz competition this year.
practice.why: This is good news, so the order is 2nd-3rd-1st person: you, he and I.

a.note: 'I' is placed first, which is the order used only for admitting a fault, not for good news.

d.note: This puts 'I' before 'he', which breaks the fixed 2nd-3rd-1st order for good news.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
[[He, you and I]] have broken the office window by mistake.
practice.why: The sentence admits a fault, so the order is 1st-2nd-3rd person: I, you and he.

b.note: This uses the good-news order (2nd-3rd-1st), but the sentence is admitting a fault.

d.note: This follows no recognised order either.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The company announced that ___ profits had doubled this quarter.
practice.why: Possession is meant here ('belonging to the company'), so the possessive pronoun 'its' is used, with no apostrophe.

a.note: 'It's' always means 'it is' or 'it has'; it cannot show possession.

c.note: 'Its'' is not a recognised form; the possessive pronoun 'its' never takes an apostrophe at all.

d.note: 'Their' is plural and does not agree with the singular 'the company' used as one body.

practice.text:
Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
The cat licked / it's paws clean / before curling up / on the warm windowsill.
practice.why: Possession is meant ('belonging to the cat'), so it should be 'its paws', with no apostrophe; 'it's' always means 'it is/has'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The two rival candidates refused to even look at ___ during the debate.
practice.why: Exactly two candidates are involved, so the correct phrase is 'each other'.

a.note: 'One another' is kept for more than two; only two candidates are named here.

c.note: 'Themselves' would mean each candidate looked at his own self, not at the other candidate.

d.note: 'One other' is not the fixed reciprocal phrase; it is 'one another'.

practice.text:
Choose the most suitable option to replace the highlighted part of the sentence:
All the five members of the panel respect [[each other]] deeply.
practice.why: Five members are involved, more than two, so the correct phrase is 'one another'.

b.note: 'Each other' is kept for exactly two; this sentence names five members.

c.note: 'Themselves' would mean each member respects his own self, not the other members.

d.note: 'One other' is not the fixed reciprocal phrase; it is 'one another'.
